hints: Think about direction of bonding - do phosphodiester bonds hold the two opposite strands together, or do they link neighbours along the same strand?
walkthrough:
Recall what a phosphodiester bond does**
Think of a single strand of DNA or RNA as a chain of beads. Each bead is a nucleotide, and the string holding one bead to the next bead along the same chain is the phosphodiester bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the pentose sugar of the next.

Apply this to Fig. 3.1**
Here you are looking across the gap between a DNA strand on the left and an RNA strand on the right during transcription. Only one nucleotide from each side is shown, and the interaction across the middle is hydrogen bonding between bases. Because no two adjacent nucleotides along the same strand are linked in the diagram, and each circle phosphate is attached to only one pentagon sugar, no phosphodiester bond can be present.

Final answer: Phosphodiester bonds join adjacent nucleotides on the same strand to form the sugar-phosphate backbone. Fig. 3.1 shows only base pairing between two opposite strands, with each phosphate bound to only one pentose sugar.

hints: Start with shape counting - compare the number of rings in the base on the left with the base on the right, and count how many dotted lines join them in the middle.
Remember the pairing rules for transcription - a triple-bonded pair must be G with C, so work out which side must be DNA and which must be RNA from the ribose label.
Look at the simplified symbols - what do the small circle and the pentagon represent in every nucleotide diagram?
Link ring number to base type - how does a double-ring purine differ from a single-ring pyrimidine, and which base on each side fits?
walkthrough:
Identify the two bases from pairing and structure**
The right-hand sugar is labelled ribose, so the right nucleotide is RNA and the left is DNA. There are three dotted lines joining the bases, and only a G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds. So the left DNA base with the double ring is guanine and the right RNA base with the single ring is cytosine.

Describe the bonds between the bases**
The three dotted lines in the centre are hydrogen bonds between the complementary bases. They are weak individually and allow the strands to separate easily, but together they give specificity to base pairing during transcription.

Label the backbone parts**
The small circle is the phosphate group and the pentagon is the pentose sugar. On the left the pentose is deoxyribose because it is part of DNA, while on the right it is ribose because it is part of RNA.

Use purine and pyrimidine terms**
Bases with two fused rings are purines and bases with one ring are pyrimidines. Guanine on the left is a double-ring purine, cytosine on the right is a single-ring pyrimidine, and a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine to keep the width between strands constant.

Final answer: Left base is guanine in DNA, right base is cytosine in RNA; three hydrogen bonds shown as dotted lines between bases; circle is phosphate; left pentagon is deoxyribose pentose sugar; left double-ring base is a purine and right single-ring base is a pyrimidine.
